intro: American football grew from campus games. Walter Camp helped write a line of scrimmage and downs in the 1880s. The forward pass was legalized in 1906 after a wave of injuries. The IHSA crowned football champions in 1974. A school gridiron is a civic field with bleachers and lights.

Soccer has an older kicking code. The FA met in London on 26 October 1863. FIFA was founded in Paris in 1904. Uruguay hosted and won the first World Cup in 1930. Illinois boys soccer titles begin in 1972 and girls titles in 1988.

title: School Fields and World Pitches

chapters.title: The Gridiron Beside the School
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a school football field become a civic room in an Illinois town?

story.title: Lights on Painted Grass
story.kicker: Bleachers face a rectangle of painted grass before anyone sits down.
paragraphs: Friday lights click on over painted white lines. The rectangle is a gridiron. The bleachers belong to the school district. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
American football grew from campus games in the late 1800s. Walter Camp of Yale helped write rules that made a line of scrimmage and a system of downs.
Those campus games were often violent. In 1906 the forward pass was legalized as part of a wider effort to change the rules after deaths and injuries.
Illinois schools later built fields and joined an IHSA football series. The first IHSA football state champions were crowned in 1974. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
story.think: Who paid for the grass and the lights in front of those bleachers?

lessons.title: Walter Camp and a Written Line
lessons.mainIdea: Walter Camp of Yale helped shape American football rules in the 1880s, including a line of scrimmage and downs.
reading: Walter Camp played and advised at Yale. In the 1880s he pushed rules that made a line of scrimmage and a set number of downs to gain ground.
Those ideas separated the American game from rugby. The ball was put in play from a line, not only from a scrum.
Camp did not invent running with a ball. He helped write a campus code other colleges would copy.

words.d: Yale adviser often called a father of American football rules
the line from which a down begins

lessons.title: Eleven on a Side
lessons.mainIdea: American football settled on eleven players on a side.
reading: Early campus games tried different numbers. The written American game came to use eleven players on the field for each team.
Eleven is a roster number in the rules. It is not a formation to copy in this class.
Soccer also uses eleven. The rooms are still different: a gridiron is marked for downs, a pitch for a continuous kicking game.

words.d: the number of players each American football side may have on the field

lessons.title: The Forward Pass, 1906
lessons.mainIdea: The forward pass was legalized in 1906 after a wave of injuries in college football.
reading: College football in the early 1900s was brutal. Players were hurt and some died. Newspapers demanded change.
In 1906 rule makers legalized the forward pass. The change was meant to open the play and reduce mass collisions.
President Theodore Roosevelt had pressed colleges to reform the game. The 1906 paper is a safety reform as well as a new kind of throw.

words.d: a throw toward the opponent's goal line, legalized in 1906
the year the forward pass was legalized in college football

look.title: Reform on paper
look.text: After deadly seasons, college football rules in 1906 legalized the forward pass. Theodore Roosevelt had urged the colleges to change the game.

choices: injuries and deaths in college football

lessons.title: Bleachers and Lights
lessons.mainIdea: A high school football field is a civic building: grass, poles, and seats a town paid for.
reading: Bleachers are seats. Lights are poles. Both sit on district land. Friday night uses that public room after dark.
Ticket money may help. Taxes and board votes built the ground. The field is not a private backyard.
Naming who paid keeps the gridiron in the same family as the gym and the park.

words.d: open seats beside a school field
the public school body that owns the campus

lessons.title: IHSA Football, 1974
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA crowned its first football state champions in 1974.
reading: The Illinois High School Association began in 1900. Football as a state series crowned first champions in 1974.
Schools played football long before 1974. The date marks a statewide playoff paper, not the birth of the game.
IHSA football uses school fields the towns already built.

words.d: the Illinois High School Association, begun in 1900
the set of games that names an Illinois school champion

lessons.title: A Leather Helmet as an Object
lessons.mainIdea: Early football helmets were soft leather caps. Hard shells came later.
reading: Early college players often wore little on the head. Soft leather helmets appeared as the game got harder.
A helmet in a museum case is an object: leather first, then harder shells.
Equipment history tells what players put on. It does not teach how to hit.

words.d: headgear worn in football, first as soft leather
the material of early football helmets

lessons.title: Not Rugby, Not Soccer
lessons.mainIdea: American football, rugby, and association football split into different written games.
reading: In 1863 London clubs wrote association rules that banned running with the ball. Rugby clubs kept carrying.
American colleges then wrote still another code with downs and a line of scrimmage.
Three papers. Three rooms. One family of winter campus games in the 1800s.

words.d: the kicking game whose rules were written in London in 1863
the carrying game that kept running with the ball

choices: downs and a line of scrimmage

lessons.title: Mass Play and Why Paper Changed
lessons.mainIdea: Before 1906, mass formations packed bodies together. Rule makers tried to open the field.
reading: Newspaper pictures from the early 1900s show piles of players. That style was called mass play.
Reformers wanted fewer of those piles. New rules, including the forward pass, tried to spread players out.
The paper changed because bodies were being broken. That is the historical reason, not a slogan.

words.d: early football that packed many bodies into one collision
a person who pushed to change the written rules

look.title: Why the rules moved
look.text: Reports of deaths and grave injuries in college football led rule makers in 1905–1906 to ban some mass formations and to legalize the forward pass.
look.cite: 1905–06 college football crisis and rule reform accounts
look.prompt: What problem were the new rules trying to reduce?

lessons.title: A Field Plan, Not a Play Sheet
lessons.mainIdea: A school field plan shows hash marks, goal posts, and yards. It does not teach a play.
reading: Grounds crews paint five-yard lines and plant goal posts. The drawing of that rectangle is a plan of a room.
A coach's signal sheet would show who runs where. A field plan shows only the room.
Students may look at an empty field diagram the way they looked at a baseball diamond plan.

words.d: short painted marks that help place the ball
the uprights at the end of a football field

chapters.title: A Rectangle the World Can Share
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a written kicking game become a rectangle two towns can share?

story.title: One Pitch, Two Languages
story.kicker: Two towns that do not share a language still share a rectangle.
paragraphs: A soccer pitch is a long rectangle with a goal at each end. Paint makes the room. The ball stays a ball. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
People kicked balls in streets and fields long before 1863. The Football Association meeting in London that year wrote one kicking code. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.

FIFA was founded in Paris in 1904. The first World Cup was played in Uruguay in 1930. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together. The names, the place, and the year stay on the page.
Illinois schools later joined IHSA soccer series. Boys crowned a first champion in 1972. Girls crowned a first champion in 1988. The reading keeps the name, the place, and the year together.
story.think: What has to travel with the ball so two towns can play?

lessons.title: Folk Football
lessons.mainIdea: People in many countries played kicking and carrying games before anyone wrote the 1863 laws.
reading: Village games in Britain used a ball and a crowd. Some games allowed carrying. Some banned it. Shrove Tuesday football is one famous seasonal match.
Those games had local customs, not one world book. A visitor from the next county might not know the local line.
The 1863 meeting did not invent kicking. It tried to write one set of words for clubs that wanted the same kicking game.

words.d: older local kicking or carrying games played before the 1863 code
a local habit that is not yet one printed world book

lessons.title: 26 October 1863 Again
lessons.mainIdea: The Football Association first met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London on 26 October 1863.
reading: Clubs met to agree on written rules for a kicking game. They formed the Football Association.
The meeting mattered because paper can travel. A club in a new town could copy the laws instead of guessing the local custom.
Rugby clubs that wanted carrying did not join that kicking code. Two sports kept two papers.

words.d: the group formed in London on 26 October 1863
the London meeting place of the first FA meeting

lessons.title: IFAB Writes the Laws
lessons.mainIdea: The International Football Association Board writes the Laws of the Game.
reading: IFAB, not FIFA, is the keeper of the numbered Laws. Law 1 describes the field. Law 3 names eleven players. Law 5 names the referee.
FIFA organizes world competitions. The Laws are a different paper from a tournament poster.
A school pitch in Illinois can still be measured from Law 1 even when the match is only a gym-class rectangle.

words.d: the board that writes soccer's Laws of the Game
the numbered world rule book for soccer

lessons.title: FIFA in Paris, 1904
lessons.mainIdea: FIFA was founded in Paris on 21 May 1904 as a world association of national football bodies.
reading: Seven national associations met in Paris and formed FIFA. England's FA did not join that first day.
FIFA is an office of offices. It does not replace IFAB's Laws.
A world body made it easier to arrange matches across borders.

lessons.title: Uruguay, 1930
lessons.mainIdea: The first FIFA World Cup was played in Uruguay in 1930. Uruguay won.
reading: Thirteen teams entered. Games were played in Montevideo. Uruguay, the host, won the final against Argentina.
The trophy later took Jules Rimet's name. The tournament became soccer's largest national-team meet.
1930 is a world date. 1863 is the code date. 1904 is the office date.

words.d: FIFA's tournament among national teams, first held in 1930

lessons.title: A Pitch Anyone Can Draw
lessons.mainIdea: Law 1 describes a rectangular field with goals. Two towns can mark that shape without sharing a language.
reading: The pitch has touchlines, goal lines, and a center mark. The goals face each other.
Paint does the introducing, the way a baseball diamond's bags do. The words in Law 1 tell a grounds crew what to paint.
A school field may be smaller than a World Cup pitch. The idea of a shared rectangle still holds.

words.d: the rectangle used for soccer
the Law that describes the field of play

1988 sits after Title IX in 1972, but the two papers are not the same document.

lessons.mainIdea: An Illinois gym-class rectangle is a smaller cousin of the World Cup pitch.
reading: Teachers paint or cone a rectangle. Two goals or two cones stand at the ends.
The idea is Law 1 at school size: a shared shape, a ball, a referee or a teacher with a whistle.
The words still travel. The grass may be shorter. The code is the same family.
